segments.title: Cost efficiency and capability efficiency answer different questions
segments.summary: The opening distinction separates a cheap purchase from a government's ability to retain a capability it may need.
segments.body: Cost efficiency asks whether a purchase gives the best financial return. That measure works when the buyer can accept a less capable substitute or replace a missing item quickly. Defence policy has a different requirement because the government may need to preserve a capability before events expose its absence. A low purchase cost says little about whether the force will be available when required. Capability efficiency tests whether the planned force can deliver the necessary result, while cost efficiency tests what it costs.

evidence.note: The speaker contrasts cost efficiency with capability efficiency in government decisions.

segments.title: Why military capabilities cannot be hired at short notice
segments.summary: A comparison with commercial lorries shows why fighters, destroyers, and carrier capability cannot be treated as easily replaceable assets.
segments.body: Standard commercial lorries can often be hired or replaced when circumstances change, so a company can buy for normal demand. Fighters, destroyers, and aircraft carriers cannot be managed on the same assumption. A force sized for a plan in which everything works has no reserve when events depart from it. Even if another organisation could lend the equipment, the receiving country would still need crews trained to use it within its own systems. Procurement choices therefore have to account for readiness and trained manpower as well as the price of each platform.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts hireable commercial lorries with non-substitutable military assets and trained crews.

segments.title: Why the 1930s Royal Navy preferred more usable submarines
segments.summary: A Royal Navy idea from the 1930s asks whether a force has enough usable units to guarantee a needed capability.
segments.body: Royal Navy planners in the 1930s used capability efficiency to ask whether enough units would exist to guarantee a capability when needed. Submarine design provided a clear example. One very large submarine with a massive crew and big guns could consume the manpower that would crew three ordinary boats. Those smaller submarines were, in the Navy's view, nearly as effective for the intended purpose. Three 80-percent solutions could therefore offer more dependable coverage than one 95-percent solution. The comparison puts usable numbers and trained crews ahead of the highest possible performance from a single boat.

evidence.note: The speaker describes Royal Navy capability efficiency and the manpower trade-off between large and ordinary submarines.

segments.title: Cost efficiency remains useful, and capability still has to exist
segments.summary: The conclusion keeps cost control in view while requiring governments to preserve defence capabilities that cannot be improvised after the need appears.
segments.body: Modern decision-making often treats cost efficiency as the default measure. Cost control remains useful for many purchases and much of the time. Government still has to guarantee defence capabilities that cannot be improvised once they are needed. Accountants can optimise expenditure, yet a cheap plan fails the efficiency test if too few usable forces remain. The lorry and submarine examples lead to a practical rule: assess the price and whether the required capability will actually be available.

evidence.note: The speaker says cost efficiency is useful much of the time but capability efficiency remains necessary.
